cards.q: What is the working definition of mesenteric venous thrombosis (MVT)?
cards.a: Thrombosis within the superior mesenteric vein, with or without extension into the portal or splenic vein.
cards.x: Acute MVT may occur with obstruction of the SMV, IMV, splenic vein or portal vein.

cards.q: Which venous segments are most often involved together?
cards.a: Portal vein + SMV most often, followed by the splenic vein and inferior mesenteric vein.
cards.x: Concomitant involvement of more than one venous segment is frequent.

cards.q: What defines <u>acute</u> MVT (AMVT)?
cards.a: Symptom onset within four weeks of presentation.
cards.x: The four-week cut-off is explicitly arbitrary.

cards.q: What defines <u>chronic</u> MVT (CMVT)?
cards.a: Symptoms for more than four weeks without bowel infarction — or MVT found incidentally on imaging.

cards.q: What is venous mesenteric ischaemia (VMI)?
cards.a: The acute onset of symptoms in the presence of AMVT.
cards.x: This clinical entity, not the radiological clot, is the main focus of the guideline.

cards.q: Are acute and chronic MVT different diseases?
cards.a: No — successive stages of the same disease with the same causes, but they need different management.

cards.q: Name the four conditions ESVS Chapter 7 explicitly <u>excludes</u>.
cards.a: Budd–Chiari (± cirrhosis) · isolated portal vein obstruction · sinusoidal obstruction (hepatic veno-occlusive disease) · hepatic disorders from heart failure or chemotherapy.

cards.q: ESVS class wording: I, IIa, IIb, IIIa, IIIb?
cards.a: I = is recommended · IIa = should be considered · IIb = may be considered · IIIa = is not indicated · IIIb = is not recommended.

cards.q: What does ESVS Level C evidence mean?
cards.a: Consensus of experts, low-quality studies (small retrospective series, case series), or a meta-analysis of such studies.

cards.q: How many of the 11 MVT recommendations reach Level B?
cards.a: Two — Rec 46 (investigate the cause) and Rec 52 (three to six months of anticoagulation).
cards.x: The other nine are Level C. None is Level A.

cards.q: What share of all acute mesenteric ischaemia is due to AMVT?
cards.x: It is the least common cause of acute mesenteric ischaemia.

cards.q: How often does AMVT appear among emergency department admissions?
cards.a: About 1 in 1000 emergency department admissions.

cards.q: Incidence of VMI in the Swedish population study?
cards.a: 2.7 per 100 000 person-years.
cards.x: 402 patients, with an autopsy rate of 87%.

cards.q: Incidence of VMI in Finland?
cards.a: 0.5 per 100 000 person-years.
cards.x: Compare Sweden's autopsy-based figure of 2.7 per 100 000.

cards.q: Mean age and sex distribution at presentation?
cards.a: Mean age 45–62 years; only 34.3% female (95% CI 30.5–38.5%).
cards.x: A male-predominant disease.

cards.q: What is the current in-hospital mortality of AMVT?
cards.a: Around 10%.
cards.x: It has fallen over recent decades.

cards.q: Mortality: AMVT vs acute arterial AMI vs NOMI?
cards.x: MVT is by far the most survivable of the three.

cards.q: In the AMESI study, what proportion of adult admissions were acute VMI?
cards.x: A worldwide multicentre prospective observational study.

cards.q: On thorough investigation, how many MVT patients have a <u>systemic</u> prothrombotic factor?
How many MVT patients have a <u>local</u> triggering factor?
How many MVT cases remain unprovoked (idiopathic)?
Name the three <u>permanent</u> risk factors ESVS lists for MVT.
cards.a: Solid cancer · liver cirrhosis · myeloproliferative disease.

cards.q: Name the four <u>transient</u> risk factors ESVS lists for MVT.
cards.a: Abdominal inflammation or infection · recent surgery · hormonal therapy · trauma.

cards.q: Pooled prevalences (1725 patients): cirrhosis/portal hypertension, liver disease, pancreatitis, IBD?
cards.a: Cirrhosis/PHT 28.8% · liver disease 27.8% · pancreatitis 11.1% · IBD 10.0%.

cards.q: Which inherited thrombophilias are over-represented in MVT (systematic review of 14 studies)?
cards.a: Prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin deficiency and protein S deficiency.
cards.x: Higher than in both the general population and patients with a single VTE elsewhere.

cards.q: Which two infections are linked to AMVT?
cards.a: Cytomegalovirus and severe SARS-CoV-2.
cards.x: CMV may act synergistically with a prothrombin G20210A mutation.

cards.q: What is the JAK2 mutation prevalence in AMVT?
cards.a: 32.7% (95% CI 25.5–35.9%) — against about 1% in VTE at other sites.

cards.q: What is the odds ratio for the association between JAK2 and MVT?
cards.x: A very large association, measured imprecisely.

cards.q: Of MVT patients carrying JAK2, how many were later diagnosed with an MPN?
cards.a: 52% (95% CI 38–67%) — with MVT as the first manifestation.

cards.q: When does ESVS say to screen for JAK2 V617F?
cards.a: In MVT without evidence of other major systemic or local risk factors.

cards.q: Which myeloproliferative neoplasms commonly present first with AMVT?
cards.a: Polycythaemia vera and essential thrombocythaemia.

cards.q: Who should be tested for thrombophilia after AMVT?
cards.a: Selected patients who will stop anticoagulation after three to six months.
cards.x: Rec 48 · Class IIb, Level C.

cards.q: MVT plus another indication for lifelong anticoagulation (e.g. AF). Test for thrombophilia?
cards.a: No — there is no indication, because the result cannot change management.

cards.q: Who should be investigated for antiphospholipid syndrome?
cards.a: Patients with recurrent MVT and recurrent foetal loss.
cards.x: Rec 47 · Class IIa, Level C.

cards.q: Which assays does ESVS list for APS and thrombophilia testing?
cards.a: Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, β2-glycoprotein antibodies; antithrombin, protein C, protein S.

cards.q: What does ASH 2023 advise on thrombophilia testing in MVT?
cards.a: Conditional testing for patients who would stop anticoagulation after three to six months.
cards.x: Very low certainty of evidence about effects.

cards.q: Is there a reliable biomarker for MVT?
cards.a: No. A single lactate or D-dimer to confirm or exclude acute mesenteric ischaemia is Class IIIb — not recommended.

cards.q: How did the D-dimer advice change from 2017 to 2025?
cards.a: 2017 recommended D-dimer to rule out AMI. 2025 is Class IIIb against any single biomarker to confirm or exclude it.

cards.q: What is the mean duration of symptoms at presentation in AMVT?
In more than 75% of cases, how long do symptoms persist before diagnosis?
cards.a: Two to three days.

cards.q: What share of patients with SMV involvement are symptomatic?
cards.a: 92% — in contrast to isolated portal vein thrombosis.

cards.q: Untreated SMV thrombosis: risk of haemorrhagic bowel infarction?
What are the most common symptoms of MVT?
cards.a: Abdominal pain, anorexia and diarrhoea.
cards.x: Pain is non-specific early; localised tenderness develops later.

cards.q: What do fever and peritoneal signs indicate in MVT?
cards.a: Progression of ischaemia to bowel infarction.
cards.x: They are the complication, not the presentation.

cards.q: What share of MVT presents acutely?
cards.a: 20–74%, depending on the vein segment involved.
cards.x: Acute presentation is more common when the mesenteric veins are involved.

cards.q: What is pylephlebitis?
cards.a: Infectious thrombophlebitis of the portal vein and its branches — high fever, malaise, abdominal tenderness, sepsis.
cards.x: May come with liver abscesses; follows appendicitis, pancreatitis or diverticulitis.

cards.q: What is a portal cavernoma?
cards.a: Chronic MVT in which the obstructed portal vein is replaced by a network of collateral veins.
cards.x: Complete portal vein occlusion is virtually always associated with portal hypertension.

cards.q: What are the classical (but rare) presentations of a cavernoma?
cards.a: Ruptured oesophageal or gastric varices, or portal cholangiopathy — jaundice, cholangitis, cholecystitis, pancreatitis.

cards.q: What is the imaging investigation of choice for suspected MVT?
cards.a: Contrast-enhanced CT with arterial and portal venous phases (optional non-contrast run).

cards.q: What slice thickness does the CTA protocol specify?
cards.a: Three-phase CTA with 1 mm maximum slice thickness.

cards.q: Which CT phase shows the extent of the venous thrombosis?
cards.a: The portal venous phase.
cards.x: It also shows the secondary bowel findings.

cards.q: Name the five non-vascular CT findings to look for.
cards.a: Bowel wall thickening · bowel dilatation · mesenteric fat stranding · pneumatosis intestinalis · portal venous gas.

cards.q: Is duplex ultrasound enough to diagnose MVT?
cards.a: No — it cannot show the extent of thrombosis or the bowel changes, and must be complemented by CT.

cards.q: Why write "?mesenteric ischaemia" on the CT request?
cards.a: Stating the suspicion is associated with better diagnosis and outcomes.
cards.x: New Class I Rec 32.

cards.q: Should CTA wait for renal function results?
cards.a: No — urgent CTA is recommended regardless of renal function.
cards.x: Rec 33 · Class I.

cards.q: What is the hardest diagnostic judgement in AMVT?
cards.a: Telling reversible from irreversible intestinal ischaemia — notably difficult, especially in AMVT.

cards.q: What is the first-line treatment for every AMVT patient without a major contraindication?
cards.a: Unfractionated or low molecular weight heparin.
cards.x: Start soon after diagnosis.

cards.q: Why is unfractionated heparin favoured in the acute phase?
cards.a: It can be reversed with protamine if laparotomy becomes necessary or bleeding occurs.

cards.q: How often does early anticoagulation achieve recanalisation?
cards.a: In 40–80% of patients.
cards.x: Complete recanalisation is associated with less extensive thrombosis.

cards.q: What are the goals of treating AMVT?
cards.a: Stop propagation and promote recanalisation — to prevent bowel infarction, portal hypertension and recurrence.

cards.q: What extra goals apply in chronic MVT?
cards.a: Preventing and treating GI bleeding and portal cholangiopathy.

cards.q: What supportive care starts immediately?
cards.a: Pain control, fluids and electrolytes, bowel rest.
cards.x: Add NG aspiration for ileus or vomiting, transfusion for bleeding, parenteral nutrition.

cards.q: Are antibiotics routine in MVT?
cards.a: No — no mortality or length-of-stay benefit shown.
cards.x: Give them for perforation, sepsis from bacterial translocation, pylephlebitis or septic thrombophlebitis.

cards.q: What is the single decision point at presentation in the ESVS algorithm?
cards.a: Peritonitis? Yes → laparotomy. No → anticoagulation plus supportive care.

cards.q: Anatomically, when does bowel infarction become likely?
cards.a: When the venous arcades and vasa recta are involved, causing complete venous occlusion.

cards.q: Most patients with AMVT are cured by…?
cards.a: Therapeutic anticoagulation and supportive treatment alone.
cards.x: Endovascular therapy and surgery are escalation steps.

cards.q: When should endovascular thrombolysis or thrombectomy be considered?
cards.a: When the patient deteriorates during anticoagulant therapy.
cards.x: Not simply because the clot is large.

cards.q: Name the endovascular options for AMVT.
cards.a: TIPS + aspiration thrombectomy · direct thrombolysis ± angioplasty · percutaneous transhepatic thrombectomy or thrombolysis · thrombolysis via the SMA.

cards.q: Direct venous vs SMA route for thrombolysis — which is preferred?
cards.a: The direct venous route — used in more centres and may be more effective.

cards.q: Transjugular or transhepatic access: mean time to thrombus resolution?
cards.a: A mean of 40 hours.

cards.q: Thrombolysis systematic review (480 patients): complete recanalisation, bleeding, bowel resection?
Clinical effectiveness: anticoagulation vs endovascular treatment?
cards.a: 89% vs 93% — but low-quality evidence with obvious selection bias.

cards.q: What are the indications for open surgery?
cards.a: Persisting or worsening symptoms, organ failure, perforation or peritonitis.

cards.q: What is the aim of surgery in AMVT?
cards.a: Remove irreversibly ischaemic bowel and preserve as much bowel as possible.

cards.q: Bowel resection rate in AMVT (systematic review of 599 patients)?
cards.x: Rates vary widely between studies.

cards.q: What are the two hard problems of surgery in AMVT?
cards.a: When to operate, and when a bowel segment is irreversibly injured.

cards.q: What unresolved research question does ESVS name for MVT?
cards.a: The value of endovascular treatment when anticoagulation fails in extensive mesenteric or portal thrombosis.

cards.q: When can a vitamin K antagonist usually be started after AMVT?
cards.a: Two to three weeks after onset, once the acute ischaemic phase has passed.

cards.q: What is the estimated one-year recurrence after AMVT?
What is the minimum duration of anticoagulation for all AMVT?
cards.a: Three to six months of a VKA or LMWH.
cards.x: A DOAC may be considered as an alternative.

cards.q: AMVT with a <u>transient</u> risk factor. Stop at six months?
cards.a: Consider extending beyond six months.
cards.x: VKA: should be considered (IIa). DOAC: may be considered (IIb).

cards.q: AMVT with a <u>permanent</u> risk factor — duration?
cards.a: Indefinite anticoagulation.
cards.x: Class I, based on consensus.

cards.q: <u>Idiopathic</u> AMVT — duration?
cards.a: Indefinite anticoagulation.
cards.x: Class I, based on consensus. Check that JAK2 was tested first.

cards.q: Why is extending anticoagulation for <u>transient</u> factors counterintuitive?
cards.a: In most VTE, a resolved transient factor means stop at three months. In MVT, recurrence can mean extensive bowel loss and short bowel syndrome.

cards.q: What three things must be balanced when deciding on extended anticoagulation?
cards.a: Bleeding risk (varices, low platelets, prior bleeds) · recurrence risk (persisting factors, prior VTE) · consequences of recurrence (bowel involvement, short bowel).
cards.x: A shared decision with the patient.

cards.q: Which DOACs have small retrospective data after AMVT?
cards.a: Rivaroxaban and apixaban — possibly as effective as VKA or enoxaparin.
cards.x: Their use is off-label.

cards.q: IPD meta-analysis (1635 patients): recurrent VTE on vs off anticoagulation?
cards.a: 3.4 vs 6.6 per 100 patient-years.
cards.x: Mean anticoagulation 316 days.

cards.q: Same IPD meta-analysis: major bleeding on vs off anticoagulation?
cards.a: 3.1 vs 5.8 per 100 patient-years.
cards.x: Higher after stopping, which points to confounding: sicker patients stop and bleed.

cards.q: In the IPD meta-analysis, what share of recurrences were in the mesenteric veins?
International registry (604 patients): thrombotic events on vs off anticoagulation?
cards.a: 5.6 vs 10.5 per 100 patient-years.

cards.q: Same registry: major bleeding on vs off anticoagulation?
cards.a: 3.9 vs 1.0 per 100 patient-years.
cards.x: The opposite direction to the IPD meta-analysis.

cards.q: Which subgroup had the highest rates of both thrombosis and bleeding?
cards.a: Cirrhosis — 11.3 thrombotic and 10.0 major bleeding events per 100 patient-years.

cards.q: Which subgroup had the lowest rates of thrombosis and bleeding?
cards.a: MVT secondary to transient risk factors.

cards.q: Anticoagulation vs stopping (meta-analysis): effect on recanalisation, bleeding, mortality, recurrence?
cards.a: Recanalisation RR 2.39 · bleeding RR 0.73 · mortality RR 0.45 · recurrence RR 0.91 (no difference).

cards.q: VKA vs DOAC in 102 MVT patients: recanalisation and major bleeding?
cards.a: Recanalisation 71% vs 69%; major bleeding 14.3% vs 9.1%.
cards.x: No significant difference except more GI bleeding with DOACs.

cards.q: Rivaroxaban cohort (96 patients): recurrent VTE at three and six months?
cards.a: 2.1% at three months (two patients) · 3.1% cumulative at six months.

cards.q: Ten-year recurrence-free survival: isolated splenic vein vs isolated mesenteric vein thrombosis?
cards.x: The segment affected changes the prognosis.

cards.q: Investigating the cause of MVT — what does ESVS recommend, and how strongly?
cards.a: Investigation for the presence of an intra-abdominal malignancy, inflammatory disease, myeloproliferative neoplasm, cytomegalovirus and SARS-CoV-2 infection, and chronic liver disease is recommended for patients with mesenteric venous thrombosis.
cards.x: Thatipelli 2010 · Primignani 2010 · De Broucker 2022 · El-Hady 2023 · Elkrief 2023

cards.q: Recurrent MVT with recurrent foetal loss — what does ESVS recommend, and how strongly?
cards.a: Patients with recurrent mesenteric venous thrombosis and recurrent foetal loss should be investigated for antiphospholipid antibody syndrome.
cards.x: Thatipelli 2010 · Primignani 2010 · Elkrief 2023

cards.q: Thrombophilia testing after AMVT — what does ESVS recommend, and how strongly?
cards.a: Testing for thrombophilia may be considered in selected patients with acute venous mesenteric thrombosis who will discontinue anticoagulation treatment after three to six months.
cards.x: Middeldorp 2023

cards.q: Imaging for suspected MVT — what does ESVS recommend, and how strongly?
cards.a: Contrast enhanced computed tomography scanning with imaging in the arterial and portal phases (and optional non-contrast CT run) is recommended for patients suspected of mesenteric vein thrombosis.
cards.x: Salim 2018 · Henes 2017 — rephrased, LoE downgraded B → C

cards.q: First-line treatment of AMVT — what does ESVS recommend, and how strongly?
cards.a: Anticoagulation with unfractionated or low molecular weight heparin as first line therapy is recommended for all patients with acute mesenteric vein thrombosis.
cards.x: Wang 2022

cards.q: Deterioration on anticoagulation — what does ESVS recommend, and how strongly?
cards.a: Endovascular venous thrombolysis and mechanical thrombectomy may be considered for patients with acute venous mesenteric ischaemia who deteriorate during anticoagulant therapy.
cards.x: Acosta 2021 · Wang 2022 · Gao 2023

cards.q: Three to six months of VKA or LMWH — what does ESVS recommend, and how strongly?
cards.a: Anticoagulation for three to six months with a vitamin K antagonist or low molecular weight heparin is recommended for all patients with acute mesenteric vein thrombosis.
cards.x: Candeloro 2022 · Valeriani 2021 · Ageno 2015

cards.q: A DOAC for the first three to six months — what does ESVS recommend, and how strongly?
cards.a: Anticoagulation for three to six months with a direct oral anticoagulant as an alternative to a vitamin K antagonist or low molecular weight heparin may be considered for all patients with acute mesenteric vein thrombosis.
cards.x: Salim 2019 · Janczak 2018 · Ageno 2022 · Valeriani 2021

cards.q: Extending a VKA beyond six months for transient risk factors — what does ESVS recommend, and how strongly?
cards.a: Extended anticoagulation beyond six months with a vitamin K antagonist should be considered for patients with acute mesenteric vein thrombosis and transient risk factors for venous thrombosis.
cards.x: Candeloro 2022 · Valeriani 2021 · Ageno 2015

cards.q: Extending with a DOAC beyond six months for transient risk factors — what does ESVS recommend, and how strongly?
cards.a: Extended anticoagulation beyond six months with a direct oral anticoagulant as an alternative to a vitamin K antagonist may be considered for all patients with acute mesenteric vein thrombosis and transient risk factors for venous thrombosis.
cards.x: Valeriani 2021

cards.q: Idiopathic AMVT, or permanent risk factors — what does ESVS recommend, and how strongly?
cards.a: Indefinite anticoagulation is recommended for patients with idiopathic acute mesenteric vein thrombosis and patients with permanent risk factors for venous thrombosis.
cards.x: Consensus

cards.q: Assessing bowel viability at operation — what does ESVS recommend, and how strongly? (Ch. 5, applies to AMVT)
cards.a: Quantitative indocyanine green fluorescent imaging may be considered as an aid in the assessment of bowel viability in patients undergoing laparotomy or laparoscopy for acute mesenteric ischaemia.
cards.x: Used in only 7% of practices

cards.q: Bowel resection strategy — what does ESVS recommend, and how strongly? (Ch. 5, applies to AMVT)
cards.a: Resection without primary reconstruction and second look laparotomy for definitive treatment should be considered in patients undergoing acute mesenteric revascularisation who need bowel resection.
cards.x: Rephrased · consensus

cards.q: Antibiotics in acute mesenteric ischaemia — what does ESVS recommend, and how strongly? (Ch. 5)
cards.a: Treatment with antibiotics is recommended for patients with acute mesenteric ischaemia.
cards.x: LoE downgraded B → C. In MVT itself, antibiotics are indicated only for perforation, translocation sepsis, pylephlebitis or septic thrombophlebitis.

cards.q: A normal full blood count rules out a myeloproliferative neoplasm. True?
cards.a: False. Test JAK2 V617F.
cards.x: 52% of JAK2-positive MVT patients declared an MPN only during follow-up.

cards.q: A normal lactate makes MVT unlikely. True?
cards.a: False. No biomarker is reliable; a single lactate or D-dimer is Class IIIb.
cards.x: The CT decides.

cards.q: The CT shows a large clot. Thrombolyse?
cards.a: Not on clot burden alone. The trigger is deterioration during anticoagulation.
cards.x: Pooled bleeding with thrombolysis: 18%.

cards.q: Appendicitis explains this patient's MVT. Workup complete?
cards.a: No. Systemic factors are found in 60–70%; investigate every patient.
cards.x: Rec 46 applies to all patients with MVT.

cards.q: Transient cause, now resolved. Stop anticoagulation at three months?
cards.a: Not by default. ESVS suggests considering extension beyond six months.
cards.x: Recs 54 and 55.

cards.q: Order a full thrombophilia screen for every MVT patient?
cards.a: No. Only in selected patients who will stop anticoagulation at three to six months.
cards.x: Rec 48.

cards.q: A trial of splanchnic vein thrombosis tells you about MVT. True?
cards.a: Only partly. Isolated splenic vein thrombosis has 97% ten-year recurrence-free survival; isolated MVT only 60%.
cards.x: Always ask which veins were studied.

cards.q: Duplex ultrasound shows SMV thrombus. Enough to plan treatment?
cards.a: No. Duplex cannot show the full extent or the bowel changes — get the CT.
